tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Map each complex value $s=\sigma+j\omega$ onto the $s$-plane and interpret $\sigma$ as exponential weighting and $\omega$ as the Fourier-frequency coordinate.

image_slots.image_description: Create a single $s$-plane diagram with origin, real axis labeled $\sigma$, imaginary axis labeled $j\omega$, and a generic point at $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

blocks.text: You have already seen $s=\sigma+j\omega$. The new geometric move is to anchor each complex value on a shared coordinate map so the same point tells you exponential weighting and oscillation at a glance.

Define the horizontal axis as the real part $\sigma$ and the vertical axis as $j\omega$ (where $\omega$ is the frequency coordinate). In this view, each point is the ordered pair $(\sigma,\omega)$, so the two labels are read separately and directly.

Use the simplest examples first: $s=0$ is the origin, $s=3$ is on the real axis at $(\sigma,\omega)=(3,0)$, and $s=j\omega$ is on the imaginary axis where $\sigma=0$. This is the base pattern students reuse.

From this point forward, movement left or right changes $\sigma$, and movement up or down changes $\omega$. A final anchor: the Fourier-frequency slice is the $j\omega$ axis, so $\sigma=0$ corresponds exactly to no exponential weighting.

image_slots.image_description: Create an $s$-plane diagram showing a labeled point at $s=2+j3$, with real axis $\sigma$, imaginary axis $j\omega$, grid lines, and projection lines touching $(2,0)$ and $(0,3)$.

example_content.example_prompt: Plot $s=2+j3$ on the $s$-plane and label the axis-crossings of the plotted point.

explanation_blocks.text: Treat the prompt as a coordinate decode: in $s=\sigma+j\omega$, the real part is the horizontal coordinate and the coefficient of $j\omega$ is the vertical coordinate.
For $s=2+j3$, identify the cue values by matching terms: $\sigma=2$ and $\omega=3$.

Place the point at two-rights, three-ups from the origin. Mark its axis crossings by drawing right-angle projections to the axes, so the same point corresponds to $\sigma$-axis intercept $(2,0)$ and imaginary-axis intercept $(0,3)$.

explanation_blocks.latex: \sigma=0 \text{ and } \omega=0\text{-axis crossings for this example are } (0,3) \text{ and } (2,0),

explanation_blocks.text: The plotted point is therefore $s=2+j3$, which is in the first quadrant and has nonzero real part, so it is not on the pure Fourier-frequency $j\omega$ axis.

example_content.example_prompt: Read the point at $\sigma=-4$, $\omega=1$ from the $s$-plane diagram and write the corresponding value of $s$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use this as a coordinate-read prompt: the point is already marked on the $s$-plane, so the task is to decode its horizontal and vertical coordinates into the canonical form $s=\sigma+j\omega$.
First, read the real-axis coordinate. The marked point lies at $\sigma=-4$, so the real part is $\sigma=-4$.
Next, read the imaginary-axis coordinate. The height is $\omega=1$, so the imaginary coefficient is positive one.
Write the point in the form $s=\sigma+j\omega$, then substitute: $s=-4+j(1)= -4+j$.
So the plotted point corresponds to $s=-4+j$, which is left of the $\sigma=0$ axis and above the real axis.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Horizontal Position as Exponential Weighting

image_slots.image_description: Create an $s$-plane with three points: $s=-2+j3$, $s=0+j3$, and $s=2+j3$; include axis labels $\sigma$ and $j\omega$, equal spacing, and clear vertical projections from each point to the axes.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the point $s=-2+j3$ and state whether it corresponds to exponential decay or growth in $e^{-st}$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use this as an interpretation prompt: the point is already given as $s$, so read its coordinates, then apply the split $e^{-st}=e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}$ to infer exponential behavior.
From the point representation, identify $\sigma=-2$ so the real part is negative.
Because $e^{-\sigma t}=e^{2t}$ grows with $t$, the weighting is exponential growth.
For comparison, if $\sigma>0$ then $e^{-\sigma t}$ decays, and $\sigma=0$ removes exponential weighting altogether (pure-frequency slice).
So the point $s=-2+j3$ corresponds to exponential growth in the $e^{-st}$ weighting term.

sections.section_title: Identifying the $j\omega$ Axis as the Fourier-Frequency Line

image_slots.image_description: Create an $s$-plane diagram with the point $s=j2$, a clearly labeled vertical axis marked as $j\omega$, and a real axis marked as $\sigma=0$. Emphasize whether the point is on the imaginary axis and include the coordinate projection to the $\sigma=0$ line.

example_content.example_prompt: From the $s$-plane, identify whether $s=j2$ is on the $j\omega$ axis and state the value of $\sigma$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the axis-check cue in the prompt: the point is given as $s=j2$, so we read its coordinates and decide whether the real coordinate is zero.
First, decompose $s=j2$ into the form $s=\sigma+j\omega$ so the real part is $\sigma=0$ and the imaginary part is $\omega=2$.
Because the real coordinate is zero, the point lies exactly on the $\sigma=0$ (or $j\omega$) axis.
That means this is the Fourier-frequency slice, so the corresponding specialization is $X(j\omega)$ with no exponential weighting shift.

prompt_blocks.text: Plot $s=-2+j3$ on the $s$-plane and choose the option that gives the correct location and coordinates.

choice_blocks.text: Right-two and up-three: $\sigma=2$, $\omega=3$, so $s=2+j3$.
Left-two and up-three: $\sigma=-2$, $\omega=3$, so $s=-2+j3$.
Left-two and down-three: $\sigma=-2$, $\omega=-3$, so $s=-2-j3$.
Right-three and up-two: $\sigma=3$, $\omega=2$, so $s=3+j2$.
Left-three and up-two: $\sigma=-3$, $\omega=2$, so $s=-3+j2$.

questions.correct_answer: The correct answer is choice $B$, because $s=\sigma+j\omega$ gives $\sigma=-2$ and $\omega=3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the real and imaginary parts: in $s=\sigma+j\omega$, the real part is the horizontal coordinate and the $j\omega$ coefficient is the vertical coordinate. So $\sigma=-2$ and $\omega=3$, giving a point at $(-2,3)$.

Left-four and down-two: $\sigma=-4$, $\omega=-2$, so $s=-4-j2$.
Left-four and up-two: $\sigma=-4$, $\omega=2$, so $s=-4+j2$.
Right-two and down-four: $\sigma=2$, $\omega=-4$, so $s=2-j4$.

questions.correct_answer: The correct answer is choice $B$, because $s=\sigma+j\omega$ gives $\sigma=4$ and $\omega=-2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The real part gives the horizontal coordinate and the coefficient on $j\omega$ gives the vertical coordinate, including sign. For $s=4-2j$, the point is $4$ units right and $2$ units down.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Horizontal Position as Exponential Weighting

image_slots.image_description: Plot the complex point at $s=-4+j1$ on the $s$-plane with axes labeled $\sigma$ (horizontal) and $j\omega$ (vertical), and mark the point clearly.
Plot the complex point at $s=3-j2$ on the $s$-plane with axes labeled $\sigma$ (horizontal) and $j\omega$ (vertical), and mark the point clearly.

prompt_blocks.text: Look at the point $s=-4+j1$ in the $s$-plane. What does the real part imply about the factor in $e^{-st}$?

choice_blocks.text: Exponential growth, since $\sigma<0$ in $s=\sigma+j\omega$.
Exponential decay, because the imaginary part is nonzero.
No exponential weighting; only oscillation from $j\omega$.
Neither growth nor decay because $\omega$ controls all time behavior.
Depends on the sign of $\omega$, not the sign of $\sigma$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $s=-4+j1$ has $\sigma=-4$. In $e^{-st}=e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}$, this becomes $e^{-(-4)t}=e^{4t}$ times oscillation, so the term grows exponentially in time.

prompt_blocks.text: For the point $s=3-j2$ shown in the $s$-plane, which description is correct for the time-domain exponential weighting in $e^{-st}$?

choice_blocks.text: Exponential decay, because $\sigma>0$ gives $e^{-\sigma t}=e^{-3t}$.
Exponential growth, since $|\sigma|$ is large.
Pure frequency-only behavior with constant magnitude because $\omega\neq 0$.
Neither growth nor decay because $\omega$ is negative.
Cannot determine behavior without the value of time step $\Delta t$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $s=3-j2$ gives $\sigma=3$, so $e^{-st}=e^{-3t}e^{j2t}$. The negative real exponent means exponential decay; $\omega$ only controls oscillation frequency.

prompt_blocks.text: From the plotted point, decide if it lies on the $j\omega$ axis and state the value of $\sigma$.

choice_blocks.text: It is on the $j\omega$ axis, so $\sigma=0$.
It is on the $j\omega$ axis, and therefore $\omega=0$.
It is off the $j\omega$ axis, so $\sigma=-2$.
It is on the real axis, so $\sigma=-2$ and $\omega=0$.
It is off-axis, so $\sigma=0$ but no Fourier interpretation applies.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $s=-2j$, the real part is zero, so this point is on the $\sigma=0$ line (the $j\omega$ axis). Therefore $\sigma=0$ and the point corresponds to the Fourier-frequency slice.

prompt_blocks.text: From the plotted point, decide if it lies on the $j\omega$ axis and state the value of $\sigma$.

choice_blocks.text: It is off the $j\omega$ axis, so $\sigma=5$ and the point is not the pure-frequency slice.
It is on the $j\omega$ axis, so $\sigma=0$.
It is on the real axis with $\sigma=0$ and $\omega=-3$.
It is off the $j\omega$ axis, and this is still a pure Fourier-frequency interpretation with no weighting.
It is on the $j\omega$ axis with $\sigma=-5$, so it still gives the frequency slice.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $s=5-3j$, the real part is $\sigma=5$ and the imaginary part is $\omega=-3$. Because $\sigma\neq 0$, the point is off the $j\omega$ axis, so it is not on the pure-frequency slice.
